“Hello, thank you for calling the Haven. My name is Elias, how can I help you today?”

The voice on the other end was hesitant, shaky, barely audible beneath a layer of static. “Hi.”

“Is this an emergency? Are you in immediate danger?” I asked, my training kicking in. Standard procedure. I’d handled countless calls like this – young people overwhelmed by depression, families struggling with addiction, people wrestling with grief and loss. Most were lost, voices swallowed by the despair that consumed them, but most were *here*, calling for a lifeline.

“I… I don’t know,” the voice said, a raw, fragile sound. “I just… I just need to talk.”

“Of course,” I said, trying to project a calm I wasn’t sure I felt. “That’s what we’re here for. Can you tell me a little bit about what’s going on?”

“It’s stupid,” the voice whispered. “Really stupid.”

“There’s no stupid way to feel. Whatever it is, we can work through it. Take your time.” I waited, listening patiently, letting the silence stretch out. Every second was precious. “What’s on your mind?”

“I’m tired,” the voice said, the exhaustion almost palpable through the phone line. “So, so tired. Of everything. Of feeling like this. Of… everything.”

“Can you be a little more specific?” I prompted gently. “What is it that’s making you feel so tired?”

“I can’t… I can’t do this anymore,” the voice choked out, a sob breaking through the static. “I just… I just want it to end.”

My gut clenched. The words hung in the air, cold and sharp. “You’re having thoughts of hurting yourself?”

There was a long pause. Then, a hesitant, shaky, “Yeah.”

“We need to save the world!” Ryder’s voice boomed, full of the saccharine enthusiasm that made my teeth ache.

I took a long, slow sip of the coffee. The irony wasn’t lost on me. Four years ago, I’d been a kid, captivated by the show. A normal kid. Now, I was a cop in Adventure Bay. And Adventure Bay, like the rest of the world, was falling apart.

Raids on the Paw Patrol headquarters, targeting the pups’ equipment and supplies. It wasn’t a coordinated attack, not at first. Just opportunistic criminals taking advantage of a town that had become complacent. Too busy enjoying their idyllic lives, too naive to realize the rot was spreading beneath the surface.

For too long, you have been taught of the men and their machinations, of the power they wielded and the chaos they created. But you have been told only a sliver of the truth. Like a constant, low-level sunburn that seemed to seep into your bones, even under layers of clothing. It wasn’t a storm either; it just continued, a diffuse, shimmering haze that rendered the world a perpetual sepia tone.

The invasion hadn’t been the spectacular, explosive affair the newsfeeds had initially promised. There’d been no blinding lasers, no roaring behemoths tearing through cityscapes. It had simply…appeared. One day, the sky was blue, the next it was filled with the glint of the Kryll ships. And then they landed.

The Kryll were…disappointing. They resembled nothing so much as walking, iridescent beetles, six-limbed and segmented, with eyes like polished obsidian. Their movements were jerky, awkward, almost comical. They wore armor that looked like layered chitin plates, polished to a dazzling sheen, and carried weapons that, it turned out, were surprisingly ineffective.

We'd anticipated, and prepared for, the worst. Nuclear arsenals, orbital defenses, a coordinated global military effort—it was all deployed, and for what? To be outmatched in almost every conceivable way. Their energy weapons, for instance, weren't designed to penetrate our defenses, just to disrupt the neural networks of the humans they encountered. A touch, a brief glance, and the victim would succumb to a paralysis so complete they could barely breathe.

The initial response, predictably, was panic. Governments crumbled. Armies evaporated. The few places that managed to hold their ground were often overrun within days, not by force, but by a creeping numbness, a silent surrender. The Kryll didn’t kill; they subjugated. They didn’t destroy; they simply...absorbed.

She’d learned quickly that the ‘terrible’ wasn’t a dragon, or a demonic horde. It was far crueler than either.

Farms had failed, mines had dried up, and the woodcutters had long since retreated to cities seeking a living. But the valley did have something, something tragically beautiful and horrifying: it had babies. And some of those babies were being sold.

Men and women who couldn’t bring themselves to love a child, who couldn't provide a home, who were simply too damaged to be parents.
